n: Jeroboam’s son Abijah falls seriously ill. His name means “the Lord is my father,” an ironic name in an idolatrous household.
In crisis, Jeroboam turns not to his calf-shrines but to the true prophet Ahijah. Yet he sends his wife in disguise, as if God’s prophet could be fooled.
She brings a modest gift—bread, cakes, and honey—as an ordinary visitor might, to keep up the disguise.
Ahijah is now blind with age. The disguise is pointless—he cannot see her anyway, and the Lord sees everything.

f.g: his eyes were fixed or dim; he was blind.

n: The Lord forewarns Ahijah who is coming and why, and what to say.
As soon as he hears her footsteps, the blind prophet greets her by name. His spiritual sight exposes her completely.
The message recalls what God did for Jeroboam: He lifted him from obscurity and made him king.
The Lord gave him the kingdom, but Jeroboam did not live like David, who kept the commandments wholeheartedly.

f.w: followed me with all his heart

n: Jeroboam has done worse than anyone before him. To “cast me behind thy back” is a vivid image of contemptuous rejection.

f.g: idols cast from metal—the golden calves.

n: Judgment will fall on every male in Jeroboam’s family, slave or free, swept away like refuse. The crude Hebrew idiom for “males” stresses total destruction.

f.w: him that pisseth against the wall
f.g: a crude idiom for every male.

f.w: him that is shut up and left

n: His family members will not even receive burial; scavenging animals will consume their bodies—the ultimate disgrace in the ancient world.
The child will die the moment she returns to the city.

A tender note in a harsh prophecy: Abijah will be the only one of the family honored with burial and mourning, because something good toward the Lord was found in him. Even in judgment God notices the righteous.

f.g: the boy’s goodness is not described, but God saw it.

n: The Lord will raise up another king to end Jeroboam’s line—and it is already under way. That king will be Baasha.

f.g: an obscure Hebrew phrase, perhaps ‘and what more? it is already happening.’

n: Ahijah looks beyond Jeroboam to the whole northern kingdom: it will be shaken like a reed in water and scattered “beyond the river” (the Euphrates). This came true when Assyria exiled Israel about two centuries later.

f.g: Hebrew Asherim: wooden poles or images for the goddess Asherah.

n: The phrase “who made Israel to sin” becomes Jeroboam’s permanent label. Leaders who lead others astray bear heavy responsibility.
She returns to Tirzah, Jeroboam’s new capital, and the child dies just as she reaches the door.

f.g: a northern city that served as Israel’s capital before Samaria.

n: All Israel mourns the boy, exactly as Ahijah foretold.
Jeroboam’s other deeds are recorded in a royal chronicle of Israel, now lost—not the biblical book of Chronicles.

f.w: the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel
f.g: lost official annals of the northern kingdom.

n: Jeroboam reigned twenty-two years (about 930–909 BC) and was succeeded by his son Nadab.
The narrative turns to Judah. Rehoboam reigned seventeen years. His mother Naamah was an Ammonite, one of Solomon’s foreign wives—a quiet hint of where Judah’s idolatry came from.
Judah also sinned, even worse than earlier generations. “Jealousy” here means God’s rightful zeal for an exclusive covenant, like a faithful spouse.
They built shrines and sacred pillars on every hill and under every leafy tree—the classic description of Canaanite worship spreading everywhere.
Cult prostitution was practiced, part of the fertility rituals of the nations the Lord had driven out.

f.g: Hebrew qadesh: male (or female) shrine prostitutes, not residents of Sodom.

n: About 925 BC, Pharaoh Shishak invaded. Egyptian inscriptions at Karnak list his campaign through Judah and Israel, one of the first biblical events confirmed outside the Bible.
Shishak carried off the treasures of the temple and palace, including Solomon’s famous gold shields. The wealth of Solomon’s age was gone within five years of his death.
Rehoboam replaced them with bronze shields—a fitting picture of glory faded into imitation.
The bronze shields were carried in ceremonial procession whenever the king went to the temple, then stored again—keeping up appearances.
Rehoboam’s other acts are recorded in Judah’s royal chronicles.
Constant border war marked the relationship between the two kingdoms.
Rehoboam dies and his son Abijam takes the throne. The repeated mention of his Ammonite mother underscores the influence of foreign worship.
